lessons.title: Why analytics needs its own model
lessons.why: "Let's have the report just read the same database as the app" — a proposal that comes up on every other project. It saves a day at the start and costs months later. Being able to explain why this isn't done comes up before you even start building the model itself.
lessons.form:
A source (OLTP) answers "what's happening with this order right now" and is optimized for writes: data is spread across dozens of narrow tables, so one change touches one row.

A reporting model (OLAP) answers "what happened across all orders over two years" and is optimized for reads: wide fact tables with small lookup tables next to them.
lessons.example:
The requester's question: "revenue by category for the quarter."

In a reporting model that's one fact table and one product lookup: sum revenue, break it down by category. Two objects, one relationship.
lessons.reads: The report reads exactly the data it needs, without getting in the way of checkout — the model refreshes at night and lives apart from the production database.
lessons.wrong: The same question, as a query straight against the production database: join orders, order_lines, products, product_categories, category_tree, and sum by the top level of the tree.
lessons.wrongWhy: It will work — right up to the day fifty people open the report at once and a heavy query collides with the same database that's handling checkout. A second bill arrives later: the source's structure changes for the app's needs, not the report's, and one day a renamed column silently breaks the reporting.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask yourself: does this query compete for resources with whatever is making money right now? If yes, there needs to be a layer between it and the source.

lessons.title: Fact grain
lessons.why: The first question for any fact table is "what does one row mean." Without an answer, you can't sum correctly or compare honestly: two tables at different levels of detail in one report give numbers that are each correct on their own and meaningless side by side.
lessons.form:
Grain is written as a list joined by a multiplication sign — one dimension per factor:

  week × outlet × SKU

If that combination occurs exactly once in the table, the grain has been named correctly.
lessons.example: fact_sellout: one row is the sales of one SKU at one outlet for one week. There are 118,449 rows, and exactly that many distinct "week × outlet × SKU" combinations.
lessons.reads: The match between row count and combination count is the proof: the key isn't duplicated, so the grain is described exactly, not approximately.
lessons.wrong: "One row of fact_sellout is one purchase."
lessons.wrongWhy: The phrasing sounds natural and is almost always wrong: a register rings up dozens of receipts a week, while the table has one row per SKU for that week. It's already an aggregate, not an event. The mistake surfaces on "how many purchases were there" — this table has no answer to that at all, and people usually bring the row count instead of an answer.
lessons.selfCheck: Check it by counting: the row count and the count of distinct combinations of the key dimensions should match. If they don't, the grain is actually finer than you thought.

lessons.title: Star and snowflake
lessons.why: An extract arrives as one wide table, with product name, brand, category, city and region sitting right next to sales. The temptation to leave it as is is real — it works, doesn't it. The star schema is why it gets split into a fact table and lookups anyway.
lessons.form:
A fact is what gets measured and accumulated: units, revenue. A dimension is what you slice it by: product, outlet, date, promo.

  fact in the center, dimensions around it — a star
  a dimension split further — a snowflake
lessons.example: fact_sellout (118,449 rows) plus dim_product (47), dim_customer (144), dim_promo (89), dim_date. The "category" attribute sits as a column inside dim_product — five categories across forty-seven products.
lessons.reads: The product name is stored 47 times — once per product — not 118,449 times, once per sales row. Editing the name happens in one place and shows up in every report immediately.
lessons.wrong: Keep one flat table of 118,449 rows, where product_name, brand, category, city and region_name sit as columns next to revenue.
lessons.wrongWhy: The most expensive thing here isn't disk space — it's consistency. Rename a product and the edit has to be carried into every row it appeared in, and any row you miss turns into a stray extra category in the filter. And the reverse case: a product that never sold this year simply doesn't exist in a table like this, so a "sales by all SKUs" report has no row for it with a zero.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask of every column in the fact table: is it measured, or does it describe? If it describes, it belongs in a lookup table, where it's stored once.

lessons.title: Relationships and cardinality
lessons.why: A relationship in a model isn't the same thing as a JOIN in a query. A JOIN combines rows; a relationship sets the direction a filter will travel along it. A report where a slicer doesn't affect half the measures is almost always explained by exactly this.
lessons.form:
A relationship has two properties, and they must not be confused:

  cardinality — how many rows on each side correspond to one row on the other (one-to-many, many-to-many)
  filter direction — lookup to fact by default, not the reverse
lessons.example: dim_product (47 rows, product_id unique) → fact_sellout (118,449 rows): one-to-many. Pick brand «Чистовъ» in a slicer — the filter travels from lookup to fact, and the revenue sum computes across that brand's five products.
lessons.reads: The "one" side filters the "many" side: the lookup sets which fact rows take part in the calculation.
lessons.wrong: Expecting a slicer on promo in dim_promo to filter dim_product the same way — "show the products that took part in the promo."
lessons.wrongWhy: The filter will reach from dim_promo into fact_sellout, and stop there: it doesn't flow back into dim_product by default — that's the "many"-to-"one" direction. The product list stays at its full 47, and that isn't a bug, it's the default behaviour — turning the reverse direction on takes a deliberate choice, and it has a cost.
lessons.selfCheck: Before you get surprised by a number, trace the filter's path with your finger from the slicer to the table where the measure computes. Did it get there, and did it change direction along the way?

lessons.title: Two paths to the same table
lessons.why: The most expensive modeling mistake looks harmless: another relationship got added because "it's more convenient to filter this way." After that, the report either refuses to compute, or — worse — computes and returns a number several times bigger than the real one.
lessons.form: There should be exactly one path from a fact table to a lookup. If there are two, the model doesn't pick the better one — it either bans the second relationship (leaves it inactive), or, if the join is made directly in a query, multiplies rows across every match.
lessons.example: fact_sellout links to dim_promo by promo_id — that's the correct path: a sales row either has a promo or it doesn't. The table's total revenue is ₽126,911,191, and along this path it stays that way.
lessons.reads: One path, one value. Every sales row corresponds to exactly one promo, or none.
lessons.wrong: Add a second path: fact_sellout → dim_product by product_id, then dim_product → dim_promo by brand, because "a promo is set up per brand anyway."
lessons.wrongWhy: Each of the nine brands has 9 to 11 entries in the promo lookup, so every sales row matches all of its brand's promos at once. Row count becomes 1,173,847 instead of 118,449, and revenue becomes ₽1,262,668,596 instead of ₽126,911,191 — exactly tenfold. No single row is "wrong" in this: the join did precisely what it was asked to do.
lessons.selfCheck: Count the paths from a fact table to a lookup. More than one — either delete the extra one, or leave it inactive and switch it on explicitly inside a measure.

lessons.title: Measure or calculated column
lessons.why: Both approaches produce what looks like the same number in the field list, and confusing the two is the source of the single most common complaint: "the report shows the wrong thing once I add a slicer." It isn't a calculation mistake — a column and a measure answer different questions.
lessons.form:
A calculated column computes once at data refresh, is stored physically per row, and afterward behaves like ordinary data — a filter doesn't recompute it.

A measure doesn't store a value at all: it recomputes every time it's displayed, accounting for whatever filters are in effect at that moment.
lessons.example: Brand «Чистовъ»'s share of revenue is 12.7% across the whole database. Set up as a measure, it's DIVIDE(Chistov revenue, total revenue). Add a region slicer for «Москва» to the report — the measure recomputes and shows 19.1%, because both parts of the formula recomputed along with the slicer.
lessons.reads: A measure doesn't store the number "12.7%" anywhere — it stores a formula and evaluates it under whatever filter is in effect right now.
lessons.wrong: Set up the same share as a calculated column: compute it once across the whole database and put 12.7% into every fact row.
lessons.wrongWhy: After a Moscow slicer, the column doesn't recompute — it holds the number that was written into it, not a formula, and it keeps showing 12.7% where the report expects 19.1%. Nothing about this looks wrong from the outside: there's a number, it looks plausible, and without checking against an independent calculation, a swap like this can go unnoticed for months.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask of every number in the model: does it have to change with a slicer, or not? Changes — a measure. Never changes (a product's category, say) — a column or a lookup attribute.

lessons.title: Filter context
lessons.why: The same measure shows different numbers in different cells of a report, and it isn't different formulas — it's different conditions the formula computes under. Being able to list those conditions for a specific cell is a basic skill for reading any report, not just your own.
lessons.form:
A cell's filter context is made up of everything acting on it at once:

  the matrix row, the matrix column,
  slicers on the page,
  filters built into the measure itself
lessons.example: A cell at the intersection of row «Москва» and a «Чистовъ» slicer: filter context is region = «Москва» AND brand = «Чистовъ». Revenue in that cell is ₽819,771. Remove the brand slicer — the context narrows to one condition, region = «Москва», and the same measure shows ₽3,718,723, the total across every brand.
lessons.reads: A cell doesn't "hold" a number — it sets the conditions a measure computes it under. Different cells in the same table almost always live in different filter contexts.
lessons.wrong: Assume that since it's the same measure (Revenue), the number must be the same in every cell of the report.
lessons.wrongWhy: A measure is a formula, not a result. The same formula, evaluated in different filter contexts, legitimately and expectedly gives different numbers: that isn't a bug, it's the whole reason measures exist — they don't need a separate formula for every slicer.
lessons.selfCheck: Before reading a number out of a cell, say out loud every condition acting on it: from the row, from the column, from the page's slicers. Miss one, and you won't understand where the number came from.

lessons.title: Row context
lessons.why: A calculated column meant to return one specific row's revenue instead shows the same huge number in every row at once. The cause is confusing two kinds of context, and without understanding that, the mistake looks inexplicable.
lessons.form:
A calculated column has row context: it "sees" the current row's values and can reference them directly.

But an aggregating function like SUM inside that column ignores row context — it only responds to filter context, and at the moment the column computes, there is none at all.
lessons.example: fact_sellout's first row: revenue = ₽398.31. A column "=SUM(fact_sellout[revenue])" in that same row shows not 398.31, but 126,911,191 — the sum of revenue across the whole table, because SUM is bounded by nothing except a filter, and there is none.
lessons.reads: A plain reference to the current row's column, with no aggregating function, is what genuinely uses row context: "=fact_sellout[revenue]" returns exactly 398.31.
lessons.wrong: Write a column "RowRevenue = SUM(fact_sellout[revenue])", expecting to get that row's own value.
lessons.wrongWhy: SUM is an aggregating function, built to add up a set of rows, not read one. Without an explicit transition from row context to filter context (that's what CALCULATE does), SUM sees an empty row context and aggregates whatever isn't filtered — meaning the entire table.
lessons.selfCheck: Does the calculated column's formula have an aggregating function (SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT)? If so, and you haven't wrapped it in CALCULATE — the result almost certainly isn't what you expected.

lessons.title: Measure additivity
lessons.why: Not every measure can be summed across every breakdown and give a meaningful number. The confusion here isn't about DAX syntax — it's about arithmetic: summing stock on hand the same way as revenue gives you a number that describes nothing.
lessons.form:
An additive measure sums across any dimension without losing meaning — revenue, units.

A semi-additive one sums across some dimensions and not across time — stock on hand.

A non-additive one doesn't sum at all — price, share, an average.
lessons.example: One distributor's stock for one SKU: October 768, November 1,055, December 1,315 — climbing, a sign of stockpiling ahead of a bonus. Summing these three months into a "quarterly stock total" is meaningless: you get 3,138, a number that never once existed in the warehouse at any moment in time.
lessons.reads: Stock sums perfectly normally across products and distributors within the same month — that's a horizontal slice. Summing it across months, along time, doesn't work: months aren't independent portions, they're snapshots of the same inventory.
lessons.wrong: Show "stock on hand for the year" on a report as SUM(units_on_hand) across all twelve months of 2025.
lessons.wrongWhy: The annual sum gives 370,142 — while actual stock at end of December was 52,350. A number sevenfold off the truth was arrived at with perfectly honest arithmetic — the question was simply put to the wrong function: annual stock is a value at a specific moment (usually period end), not a sum of monthly snapshots.
lessons.selfCheck: Before writing SUM, ask: does this quantity accumulate over a period (like revenue), or exist at every moment in time (like stock, price)? The second kind can't be summed across time.

lessons.title: The date table
lessons.why: The model already has dates — right there in the fact tables. It seems like a separate calendar shouldn't be needed: filter on those columns and you're done. The trap is that the date in one fact table and the date in another aren't the same column, and without a shared calendar there's no way to bring them under one slicer.
lessons.form:
A date table is a by-day lookup, with derived columns (week, month, quarter, year), connected to every fact table at once.

One slicer on this table filters every fact table simultaneously, even when they have different native time granularity.
lessons.example: dim_date's row for March 3rd 2025: date_id = week_start = 2025-03-03, while its own month_start = 2025-03-01, quarter = 1. This one row connects fact_sellout (whose week starts March 3rd) and fact_sellin (whose month starts March 1st) — both see the same calendar, just through different columns of it.
lessons.reads: One "quarter = 1" slicer filters weekly sales and monthly shipments at the same time — because both fact tables ultimately connect to the same date table.
lessons.wrong: Skip dim_date: build a slicer straight on week_start in fact_sellout, and expect it to affect fact_sellin the same way.
lessons.wrongWhy: fact_sellin has no row with date 2025-03-03 at all — the whole of March sits in one row dated 2025-03-01 there. A slicer built on one fact table's column finds no matches in the other: they literally hold different values in different columns, and no direct relationship between the two fact tables resolves that difference.
lessons.selfCheck: How many fact tables does your model have, and how many different time granularities among them (week, month)? More than one, and you need a shared calendar — otherwise one slicer will never tie them all together.
